name: IMO FAQ on autonomous shipping and the MASS Code
title: IMO FAQ on autonomous shipping and the MASS Code
answer: This is the International Maritime Organization's FAQ page on autonomous shipping. Its most useful point is that IMO adopted a new International Code of Safety for Maritime Autonomous Surface Ships in May 2026, effective 1 July 2026. The page defines a MASS as a ship that can operate independently of human interaction to varying degrees, but only when autonomous or remote technologies replace or support crew functions and the ship holds a valid MASS Safety Certificate. It also notes the Code is currently voluntary guidance.

sections.body: The International Maritime Organization publishes this FAQ page on autonomous shipping. It is a question and answer style overview of the IMO's work on Maritime Autonomous Surface Ships, the MASS Code and related regulatory developments. The page covers definitions, certification, safety goals, operating conditions, interim trial guidelines and the current commercial status of autonomous ships. The source text was harvested on 27 September 2026 and refers to IMO adoption of the MASS Code in May 2026 and its entry into effect on 1 July 2026.
sections.heading: What this source is

sections.body: The page explains that IMO adopted a new International Code of Safety for Maritime Autonomous Surface Ships in May 2026, and that the Code came into effect on 1 July 2026. It defines a Maritime Autonomous Surface Ship as a ship which, to a varying degree, can operate independently of human interaction. A ship is considered a MASS only when autonomous or remote technologies replace or support functions normally carried out by crew on board. To qualify, it must complete the approval process and hold a valid MASS Safety Certificate. Enhanced automation alone does not make a ship a MASS. Shipowners, operators and designers are encouraged to take a functional approach, assessing which functions are remote, autonomous or conventional, in compliance with SOLAS. The page says autonomous systems present different operational risks and require an alternative approach. The MASS Code provides voluntary guidance for safe design, operation and certification, complements existing regulations, focuses on safety goals, maintains technology neutrality and is designed to facilitate a future transition into a mandatory instrument. It introduces concepts for operating conditions and limitations, including wind speed, sea state, visibility, water depth, adverse weather and daytime versus nighttime operations, and actions if conditions move outside those limits. Before adoption, trials were conducted under interim guidelines approved by the Maritime Safety Committee in June 2019. At present no commercially operating, internationally trading SOLAS cargo ships operate autonomously or remotely controlled, though trials show larger such ships are feasible and may enter commercial service soon.
sections.heading: What it says

sections.body: The source states that IMO adopted the MASS Code in May 2026 and that it came into effect on 1 July 2026. It defines a MASS as a ship which, to a varying degree, can operate independently of human interaction, and says a ship qualifies only with a valid MASS Safety Certificate. It says enhanced automation alone does not make a ship a MASS and such ships have no privileges over conventional vessels. It notes interim guidelines were approved by the Maritime Safety Committee in June 2019 under MSC.1-Circ.1604. It states there are currently no commercially operating, internationally trading SOLAS cargo ships that operate autonomously or remotely controlled. It also mentions an IMO seminar in April 2024 on MASS implications for ports and public authorities.
sections.heading: Figures and claims worth noting

sections.body: For a reader following AI in transportation, this source is the primary regulatory reference for autonomous shipping. It shows where international rules for AI navigation, collision avoidance and crewless vessels are being written, through the MASS Code and its safety goals. It clarifies that the Code is currently voluntary guidance and that no internationally trading SOLAS cargo ships operate autonomously or remotely controlled today. It also sets out the operating conditions and limitations that autonomous systems must handle, such as wind speed, sea state, visibility, water depth, adverse weather and day versus night operations. This helps readers separate regulatory reality from trial activity and commercial claims.
sections.heading: What it means for AI in Transportation

sections.body: This is an IMO FAQ page, so it is a high level regulatory overview rather than a detailed technical or legal text. It does not reproduce the full MASS Code, article by article, and it does not give compliance deadlines beyond the May 2026 adoption and 1 July 2026 entry into effect. It does not cover national rules, port state implementation, insurance, liability or cybersecurity. It is published by an intergovernmental regulator and is not a commercial vendor document. The page is partial in that it describes the Code as voluntary guidance and notes that no internationally trading SOLAS cargo ships currently operate autonomously or remotely controlled. The supplied text was harvested on 27 September 2026.
